newsitem.title: URUGUAY: France's Chirac urges tightening of trade rules.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac urges tightening of trade rules.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac on Friday used his visit to Uruguay, which gave its name to a historic round of GATT talks, to call for a further tightening of world trade rules.

In a speech to Congress in Montevideo, he said the role of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) must be strengthened and its rules extended to major countries bidding to join such as Russia, China and Saudi Arabia.
In an apparent attack on last year's Helms-Burton law that stiffens U.S. trade sanctions on Communist-ruled Cuba, he said trade rules must be set and accepted by all countries.

"This is the reason why we must fight against the temptation of unilateralism, consolidate the multilateral system and first of all strengthen the role of the WTO," he said. The European Union strongly opposes the U.S. law.
The Uruguay round of General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) talks was launched in 1986 in the resort of Punta del Este, leading to the creation of the WTO in 1995.

Chirac said much had still to be done to end abusive trade practices, improve copyright protection and ensure basic labour rights and environmental issues are covered by trade rules. "We must see to it that the great world movement towards regional integration does not lead to fragmented and closed-up trade zones," he said.

Chirac, who is touring the four member countries of the South American Mercosur customs union, has repeated his vision of a world divided into major regional groups cooperating rather than competing against each other.

Uruguayan President Julio Sanguinetti told a news conference he supported France's call for holding the first summit of European Union and Latin American leaders next year, an initiative Chirac insists is not intended to challenge the United States in its traditional zone of influence.
From Mercosur's biggest country, Brazil, he flew to the smallest, Uruguay, which aspires to use its location at the centre of the group to gain a role as a major sea outlet.
Mercosur is to set up its headquarters in Montevideo, a sleepy port capital that Chirac said could become the equivalent of Brussels for the European Community.

Like his visit to the other Mercosur countries -- Paraguay and Argentina -- later this week, Chirac's 24-hour stay in Uruguay was intended to boost bilateral trade and relations, which slumped during the last two decades as Uruguay went through military dictatorship and Latin America's debt crisis.

French investment picked up recently. Chirac said French groups had an eye on major Mercosur infrastructure projects including a 25-mile (40-km) bridge across the Rio de la Plata estuary connecting Buenos Aires to the Uruguayan town of Colonia and a giant waterway linking the four countries.
Chirac, who was to open an assembly line for Citroen ZX cars, presided over the signing of a technical cooperation and training agreement among medium-size firms in both countries.
Uruguay has a long Francophile tradition and Chirac said he was moved to be greeted with the Marseillaise, France's national anthem, sung in French by dozens of schoolchildren.
Chirac was flying on Friday night to Cochabamba in Bolivia and on Saturday to La Paz.
